excerpt: Every one-step equation is a locked box with the answer inside. Here is the one idea that opens all four types, worked examples for each, and a quick quiz to test yourself.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Give a Grade 6 class the equation x + 7 = 12 and most of them will just see that x is 5. Change it to x − 19 = 46 and the guessing stops. That is exactly why one step equations Grade 6 students meet this year matter so much: they replace lucky guessing with a method that works every single time, no matter how ugly the numbers get. The whole method rests on one idea — do the opposite operation to both sides — and once a child owns that idea, all four types fall over like dominoes.

I tell my students to picture the equation as a balance scale. The equals sign is the pivot. Whatever sits on the left weighs the same as whatever sits on the right. If you add, subtract, multiply or divide on one side, you must do the identical thing on the other, or the scale tips and the equation stops being true.

The one rule behind every one-step equation

A one-step equation hides the letter behind a single operation. Something has been done to x — it was added to, subtracted from, multiplied or divided. Your job is to undo that operation using its inverse, and to do it to both sides so the balance holds. Addition and subtraction undo each other; multiplication and division undo each other. That is the entire toolkit.

You see in the equationInverse to apply to both sidesExample
Something added (+)Subtract (−)x + 8 = 20
Something subtracted (−)Add (+)x − 5 = 11
Multiplied (×)Divide (÷)6x = 54
Divided (÷)Multiply (×)x ÷ 4 = 9

Type 1: undoing addition

Take x + 8 = 20. Something (an 8) has been added to x, so subtract 8 from both sides:

x + 8 − 8 = 20 − 8, which leaves x = 12.

The +8 and −8 on the left cancel, leaving x alone. That cancelling to zero is the whole point — you are peeling the 8 away from the letter.

Type 2: undoing subtraction

For x − 5 = 11, a 5 has been subtracted, so add 5 to both sides:

x − 5 + 5 = 11 + 5, giving x = 16.

This is the one that trips people up. When they see a minus sign, a lot of students want to subtract again. Slow down and name the operation first: ‘5 was taken away, so I add it back.’

Type 3: undoing multiplication

In 6x = 54, the 6 sitting against the x means 6 × x. To undo multiplication, divide both sides by 6:

6x ÷ 6 = 54 ÷ 6, so x = 9.

A quick caveat from experience: many Grade 6 students read 6x as ‘six and x’ and try to subtract 6. There is no addition here, so subtraction does nothing useful. The 6 is glued to the x by multiplication, and only division unglues it.

Type 4: undoing division

For x ÷ 4 = 9 (often written as a fraction, x over 4), the x has been divided by 4. Multiply both sides by 4:

x ÷ 4 × 4 = 9 × 4, so x = 36.

Here is the counter-intuitive bit worth pointing out: dividing made the number look smaller, so students expect a small answer — yet the real value of x is the biggest number in the problem. Undoing a division should make things bigger.

Always check by substitution

This is the step most students skip and the one that saves the most marks. Once you have an answer, put it back into the original equation in place of the letter and see if both sides match.

  • For x = 12 in x + 8 = 20: 12 + 8 = 20. True.
  • For x = 16 in x − 5 = 11: 16 − 5 = 11. True.
  • For x = 9 in 6x = 54: 6 × 9 = 54. True.
  • For x = 36 in x ÷ 4 = 9: 36 ÷ 4 = 9. True.

Substitution takes ten seconds and it is honest — the numbers either balance or they do not. In an exam, a wrong answer you have checked is a wrong answer you can catch and fix before you hand the paper in.

Two habits that prevent silly errors

First, write the inverse operation on both sides on its own line, lined up under the equals sign. Doing the step mentally is where a stray sign sneaks in. Second, do the same operation to both sides at once — never touch one side, walk away, and come back. Keep the balance visibly balanced.

A note on word problems

Grade 6 exams love wrapping these in a story: ‘Riya spent ₹150 and had ₹90 left. How much did she start with?’ That is just x − 150 = 90 in disguise. Turn the words into one equation, then run the same undo-and-check method. The maths does not change — only the costume does.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

The free 8-question quiz below covers all four types — undoing addition, subtraction, multiplication and division — plus a check-by-substitution question. Try each one, then read the explanation for anything you miss. When you want longer graded practice with a full answer key, the printable worksheet linked at the end gives you plenty of it.

quiz.title: Grade 6 One-Step Equations Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions covering all four one-step types and checking by substitution. Solve each, pick your answer, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: A 9 was added, so subtract 9 from both sides: 17 − 9 = 8, so x = 8.
A 6 was subtracted, so add 6 to both sides: 15 + 6 = 21, so x = 21.
The x is multiplied by 7, so divide both sides by 7: 56 ÷ 7 = 8, so x = 8.
The x is divided by 5, so multiply both sides by 5: 6 × 5 = 30, so x = 30.

questions.q: To solve x − 12 = 4, what should you do to both sides?
questions.explanation: Subtraction is undone by addition, so add 12 to both sides. That gives x = 16.
Multiplication and division undo each other, so you divide both sides to remove a multiplier.

questions.q: You solved 4x = 32 and got x = 8. Which check by substitution proves it?
questions.explanation: Put x = 8 back in: 4 × 8 = 32, which is true, so the answer is correct.

questions.q: Riya spent ₹150 and had ₹90 left. If x is what she started with, solve x − 150 = 90.
questions.explanation: Add 150 to both sides: 90 + 150 = 240, so she started with ₹240.

faq.q: What is a one-step equation in Grade 6?
faq.a: It is an equation where a single operation has been applied to the unknown, such as x + 7 = 12 or 6x = 54. You solve it in one move by applying the inverse operation to both sides.

faq.q: How do I know which operation to undo?
faq.a: Look at what has been done to the letter. If a number is added, subtract it; if subtracted, add it; if it multiplies the letter, divide; if it divides the letter, multiply. Always do the same step to both sides.

faq.q: Why do I have to do the same thing to both sides?
faq.a: An equation is a balance. The two sides are equal, so any change you make to one side must be made to the other, or the balance breaks and the equation is no longer true.

faq.q: What does checking by substitution mean?
faq.a: Put your answer back in place of the letter in the original equation and work out both sides. If they match, your solution is correct. It takes seconds and catches mistakes before the exam does.
